analysis.one_liner: Bans unlimited 'soft money' from national political parties and tightens campaign disclosure and enforcement rules.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan campaign finance bill with 165 House cosponsors was split among six committees and never received a vote; it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred national party committees from soliciting, receiving, or spending 'soft money' — unlimited contributions from corporations, unions, and individuals that are not subject to federal contribution limits — and barred such money from federal election activity by state and local party committees. It would also have required disclosure by anyone spending more than $50,000 a year of soft money on federal election activity, tightened the definition of coordinated spending, banned fundraising on federal property, and imposed criminal penalties, including up to 10 years in prison, for knowingly taking foreign contributions.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters and small donors gain because the unlimited, largely untraceable soft-money channel that lets wealthy donors and corporations bankroll party campaigns would close. Voters would also learn who is paying for campaign activity through new disclosure requirements, and candidates who pledge to limit spending from their own wealth would get a voluntary option.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits national party committees and their agents from soliciting, receiving, directing, or spending any funds not subject to federal contribution limits, prohibitions, and reporting requirements, and applies the same restrictions to state and local party money spent on federal election activity such as voter registration, get-out-the-vote work, and ads naming federal candidates.

Requires any person outside the parties spending more than $50,000 a year of soft money on federal election activity to report it to the Federal Election Commission, with reports within 24 hours for spending made within 20 days of an election.
Blocks candidates from depositing contributions from anyone giving more than $200 a year until contributor information is complete, and lowers the disclosure itemization threshold from $200 to $50.

Criminalizes soliciting donations in federal office space, requires national parties to reimburse taxpayers at cost for political use of Air Force One, bans campaigns from handing out election-day 'walking around money,' and allows expulsion of House members convicted of taking foreign contributions.
Creates a voluntary option limiting congressional candidates to $50,000 in spending from their own and their family's funds.

analysis.who_pays: National and state party committees lose the unlimited soft-money channel; corporations, wealthy individuals, and unions that funded party soft-money accounts lose an avenue of influence; candidates who self-fund remain unconstrained unless they opt in.

drawbacks.text: The bill trades the soft-money ban for modestly higher limits: it raises the aggregate individual contribution limit from $25,000 to $30,000 per year and allows up to $10,000 a year to a state party committee, and it exempts party soft money entirely for candidates who do not accept the voluntary $50,000 personal-funds limit.

It codifies the Beck decision, requiring labor unions to give nonmember employees a procedure to object to their fees being used for political activity unrelated to collective bargaining — a provision unions opposed but the bill's Republican sponsors included.

The new express-advocacy definition carves out an exception for printed or internet 'voting record or voting guide' communications, so some campaign-style issue communications could remain outside the disclosure and funding rules the bill applies to other ads.

It adds serious new penalties, including possible imprisonment for campaign law violations and up to 10 years in prison and a $1 million fine for foreign-contribution violations, raising the stakes for inadvertent compliance errors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and hard to dispute: closing the soft-money loophole, which at the time let parties raise and spend unlimited unregulated money in federal elections, would materially reduce the leverage of the largest donors over both parties. The costs are real but smaller — slightly higher hard-money limits, a labor-law provision unions disliked, and tougher penalties — and the bill's mostly bipartisan drafting suggests both parties' members saw the trade as net worthwhile; the obstacle was never a floor vote, which is why the manner of its death matters.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to six committees, parked in a subcommittee, and never reported back out; it died without a single floor vote when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Christopher Shays introduced the bill on January 31, 2001, with 164 original cosponsors from both parties, including the House Democratic and Republican leadership of the day.

It was referred to the Committee on House Administration and five other committees — Education and the Workforce, Government Reform, the Judiciary, Ways and Means, and Rules — for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, so no single committee had a deadline to act.

On February 15, 2001, it was referred to the Oversight Subcommittee on Government Efficiency, and on March 15, 2001, to the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, where the record of action ends.
No committee ever reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled, and no further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the 107th Congress, which ended January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National party committees and their largest soft-money donors were better off in the near term: the unlimited money channel stayed open through the 2002 elections. The loss was temporary, though — a successor Shays-Meehan bill passed both chambers later in the same Congress and was signed into law as the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Party committees and big donors, temporarily

for.name: Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Bipartisan Campaign Finance Reform Act of 2001 on January 31, 2001.

for.name: Martin Meehan
for.what_they_did: Joined Shays as the lead Democratic cosponsor of the bill.

for.name: 136 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from roughly two-thirds of the House Democratic caucus.

for.name: 27 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including several senior Republicans, despite their party controlling the House.

against.name: Dennis Hastert
against.what_they_did: Allowed the bill to be referred to six committees simultaneously 'for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker' and never scheduled it for a House vote; no action of any kind followed after March 2001.

against.name: House Administration Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral (chaired by a Republican, Rep. Bob Ney)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee, and after its referral to subcommittees took no recorded action on it.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan: 164 cosponsors included 136 of 208 House Democrats, 27 of 223 House Republicans, and the House's sole Independent. No roll calls were ever taken, so the vote split was never measured; the bill was stopped by the Republican leadership's control of the committee and floor process, without a vote.

industries.industry: National and state political party committees
industries.note: The bill takes away the parties' unlimited soft-money channel for federal elections, which is their most lucrative fundraising stream, but partially compensates them by raising the state-committee limit to $10,000 and the aggregate individual limit to $30,000, and by exempting non-opting candidates from coordinated-expenditure limits. Party committees profited by channeling untraceable corporate and union money into federal races, which the disclosure provisions exist to expose.

industries.industry: Corporate and union soft-money givers (large donors and lobbying interests)
industries.note: Corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals lose the ability to give unlimited, largely unregulated money to party committees for federal election activity. Their interest in keeping that channel open runs against the public's interest in knowing who funds campaigns.

Unions lose their soft-money giving to party committees, and the bill's codification of the Beck decision obliges them to notify nonmember employees and refund the portion of their fees spent on politics. Unions otherwise supported campaign finance reform, making their overall stake genuinely two-sided.

Political advertising remains permitted, but the bill expands the definition of express advocacy and requires sponsorship disclaimers, stand-by-your-ad statements, and rapid reporting of election-season spending, tightening rules on a source of broadcast revenue without banning it.
